title: "Git LFS: pointers and large files"

# Git LFS: pointers and large files

Git Large File Storage (LFS) is a separate Git extension for versioning selected file contents outside Git's ordinary object database. It is useful for assets whose successive versions are large and hard to compress or merge. It does not replace backups or eliminate storage and bandwidth costs. Your hosting service must support LFS, and collaborators need access to both the Git repository and its LFS objects.

## What happens to a file

When you add a path matched by an LFS attribute, the LFS clean filter stores its payload locally and gives Git a small pointer containing an object ID and size. A checkout can use the filter to replace the pointer in the working tree with the payload. On push, an LFS hook normally uploads required payloads to the LFS endpoint separately from the Git objects. Thus a commit alone is not a complete backup if the LFS payloads are missing.

```text
working file → LFS clean filter → pointer in Git commit
                               → payload in local LFS store
Git push + LFS hook            → Git remote + LFS endpoint
```

## Start tracking a new type

Install the `git-lfs` package using your Linux distribution's package manager, then check `git lfs version`. In an existing repository:

```sh
git lfs install
git lfs track '*.psd'
cat .gitattributes
git add .gitattributes artwork.psd
git commit -m 'Track artwork with LFS'
git lfs ls-files
git show HEAD:artwork.psd
```

Replace `artwork.psd` with a file that exists. Quoting the pattern prevents the shell from expanding it before LFS writes it to `.gitattributes`; commit that file so collaborators inherit the rule. `git lfs install` configures LFS filters for the user and installs hooks in the current repository. If you do not want user-wide configuration, run `git lfs install --local` inside the repository. Inspect existing custom hooks before installing: a hook conflict may require manual integration.

`git lfs ls-files` lists tracked LFS objects. The last command prints the **committed pointer**, not the working file. It starts with `version https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1`, followed by an SHA-256 object ID and byte size. That URL identifies the pointer format; it is not the URL of your asset. Verify the actual working file with an appropriate viewer or checksum.

## Fetching and troubleshooting

Normally checkout downloads required LFS objects when the extension and remote access are configured. If the working file contains pointer text instead of the expected asset, first check `git lfs version`, `git lfs ls-files`, access to the configured remote, and any checkout or download errors. Once the extension and access are available:

```sh
git lfs pull
```

This fetches and checks out LFS objects for the current ref. `git lfs fetch` downloads objects without updating working files; `git lfs checkout` uses locally available objects without downloading and does not overwrite modified files. Include/exclude settings and sparse or partial checkouts can restrict what is fetched; see the [pull manual](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/blob/main/docs/man/git-lfs-pull.adoc). A missing server object, exceeded quota, or insufficient permissions requires fixing the remote situation; retrying checkout alone cannot recreate bytes that are unavailable.

## Existing files and history

`git lfs track` sets a rule; it does not rewrite earlier commits. If matching files already exist in the current snapshot, on an otherwise clean working tree use `git add --renormalize .`, inspect the staged diff and `git lfs ls-files`, then commit the conversion and `.gitattributes`. This affects the new snapshot, not earlier versions or other branches.

To remove old large Git blobs from history, [LFS migration](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/blob/main/docs/man/git-lfs-migrate.adoc) rewrites commits and changes IDs. Inventory refs and LFS storage, make and verify backups, coordinate with collaborators, and rehearse in a copy before changing a shared repository. A history rewrite and subsequent remote updates have wider consequences than the ordinary forward conversion above.

## Check yourself

- Why might a colleague receive a pointer instead of the asset? The LFS client, payload, authorization, or download may be missing; inspect the error and remote state.
- Does tracking `*.psd` retroactively shrink Git history? No. Earlier Git blobs remain until history is rewritten and old copies are eventually removed.
- Is a Git-only backup enough? No. Preserve and test restoration of both Git objects and referenced LFS payloads.

References: [Git LFS project and setup](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs), [LFS FAQ](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/blob/main/docs/man/git-lfs-faq.adoc), and [checkout manual](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/blob/main/docs/man/git-lfs-checkout.adoc).
